ticks.label: 1400 AD
ticks.name: Quattrocento threshold
ticks.era: Italian powers, Valois–Lancaster, and Ottoman rise
ticks.narrative: At 1400 Italian republics and signorie already export humanism and mercenary war while Valois and Lancastrians bleed in France. The Ottomans press the Balkans; Iberian crowns prepare the final Nasrid reduction; Burgundy is a princely third force. This tick is late medieval politics with Renaissance culture beginning in Italian courts and communes.

ticks.label: 1450 AD
ticks.name: Print, guns, and the fall of the City
ticks.narrative: Mid-century turns on Constantinople’s fall (1453), French recovery under Charles VII, and Burgundy’s glittering composite state. Italian powers balance before the French wars; print and artillery begin to alter information and sieges. The snapshot is post-plague recovery meeting Ottoman and Valois ambition.

ticks.label: 1500 AD
ticks.name: Age of discoveries & Italian Wars
ticks.era: Charles VIII’s trail, Habsburg marriages, Atlantic turn
ticks.narrative: Around 1500 French armies open the Italian Wars, Spain unites under the Catholic Monarchs’ heirs, and Portuguese routes already pull Asia into European politics. Maximilian’s Habsburg web and Tudor consolidation frame the north. Culture is High Renaissance in Italy while dynastic war makes the peninsula Europe’s battlefield.

ticks.label: 1550 AD
ticks.name: Confessions harden
ticks.narrative: By 1550 Lutheran settlement (Augsburg 1555 approaches), the Council of Trent has begun, and Charles V’s stretched empire faces Valois France and Ottoman pressure. England under Edward/Mary oscillates confessionally; Scandinavia is Lutheran; Muscovy under Ivan IV pushes east. This tick is Reformation politics—faith as border—before the Dutch Revolt ignites.

ticks.label: 1600 AD
ticks.name: Century’s turn
ticks.era: Dutch Revolt, Philip III, and northern wars
ticks.narrative: c. 1600 the Dutch Republic fights for recognition, Spain under Philip III manages a global but strained monarchy, and France exits Wars of Religion toward Henri IV’s settlement. Sweden and Poland contest the Baltic; England is late Elizabethan/early Stuart. Renaissance culture shades into confessional Baroque politics.

narrative: From Hundred Years’ War and Reconquista finales through Italian Wars, Ottoman–Habsburg collision, Reformation fracture, and the Dutch Revolt’s edge—Europe’s map is dynastic and confessional, not national.

polities.name: Kingdom of France
polities.description: From Charles VII’s reconquest to Louis XI’s ruthless statecraft, France claws back English footholds, absorbs Burgundian wreckage, and draws Brittany into the crown’s orbit. Charles VIII’s and Louis XII’s Italian adventures export French arms into the peninsula and import Italianate taste to Fontainebleau. Francis I and Henry II duel Charles V’s encirclement; after mid-century the realm fractures in the Wars of Religion—Guise zeal, Huguenot resistance, and St Bartholomew’s blood. Henri of Navarre’s conversion, coronation, and Edict of Nantes (1598) close the century with a reunited Catholic monarchy that tolerates a guarded Protestant minority. Parlements, royal fiscal-military growth, and a Paris-centered court remake the medieval patchwork into an early modern state—still short of Louis XIV’s later frontiers.
polities.conflicts: Hundred Years’ War vs England (to 1453); Armagnac–Burgundian civil strife; League of the Public Weal; Burgundian succession wars after 1477; Italian Wars vs Habsburgs (1494–1559); Habsburg encirclement under Charles V/Philip II; French Wars of Religion (1562–1598) including St Bartholomew; interventions in Scotland and the Dutch Revolt; Franco-Spanish frontier fighting into 1600. Royal governors and urban militias turn every confessional riot into a local war of banners.
polities.leaders: Charles VI; Charles VII; Joan of Arc (captain of the sacred campaign); Louis XI; Charles VIII; Louis XII; Francis I; Henry II; Catherine de’ Medici; Charles IX; Henry III; Henry IV of Navarre/Bourbon.
polities.religion: Catholic monarchy with stubborn Gallican claims over papal interference. Calvinist Huguenots build consistories and noble clienteles from the 1550s; ultra-Catholic Guise leagues answer with Rome and Spain. The Edict of Nantes (1598) grants fortified coexistence without surrendering the crown’s Catholic public face. Gallican bishops and Jesuit newcomers compete to define what a French Catholic looks like after Trent.
polities.culture: Late Gothic piety yields to Fontainebleau’s Italianate court, vernacular chronicle, and print-shop politics. Royal entries, châteaux along the Loire, and a developing absolutist ceremonial teach subjects to see the king as the realm’s center. Occitan south remains culturally distinct under northern political victory; provincial parlements guard local privilege even as taxes centralize. Loire châteaux and Paris printers teach subjects that taste and news both flow from the crown’s orbit.
polities.summary: Valois France exits the Hundred Years’ War as a bruised but consolidating territorial monarchy. Charles VII and Louis XI claw back English footholds, break Burgundian autonomy, and absorb Brittany by marriage. Sixteenth-century kings fight…
polities.story: Joan of Arc’s 1429 Loire campaign and Charles VII’s Reims consecration turn a disinherited Valois claim into sacral recovery; Formigny and Castillon (1450–53) end English Gascony. Louis XI outmaneuvers the League of the Public Weal and, after Nancy (1477), scavenges Burgundian spoils while Mary of Burgundy’s Habsburg marriage steals the Netherlands. The Italian Wars begin as dynastic opportunity and become a Habsburg–Valois meat grinder; Pavia (1525) captures Francis I and advertises Spanish tercios as the new grammar of battle. Confessional civil war after 1562 makes every governorship a fortress: Coligny’s murder and the August 1572 massacres poison trust for a generation until Nantes trades coexistence for obedience. Fontainebleau’s stuccoed galleries and Montaigne’s tower are twin emblems—court magnificence and private conscience—of a kingdom learning to be a state.
polities.literature: Froissart’s afterlife and Commynes’ memoirs harden political prose; Rabelais carnivalizes learning; the Pléiade (Ronsard, du Bellay) elevates French verse. Montaigne’s Essays invent the self as a field of inquiry; d’Aubigné’s Tragiques remember confessional war in verse of ash and scripture. Satire and memoir become weapons; the essay joins epic as a national form.

Gallicanism—crown over church courts; politique arguments for civil peace; Bodin’s sovereignty theory (Six Books of the Commonwealth); neoclassical taste imported with Italian Wars veterans and artists.
polities.ideas: Gallicanism argues a French church under the crown; Bodin’s Six Books of the Republic theorizes sovereignty amid civil war. Politiques invent confessional truce as reason of state—order before purity—paving Henri IV’s settlement. Gallican lawyers and politiques turn civil war into a laboratory of sovereignty theory. Sovereignty talk hardens as leagues and politiques argue whether peace is betrayal.
polities.artIdeas:

Gallicanism—crown over church courts; politique arguments for civil peace; Bodin’s sovereignty theory (Six Books of the Commonwealth); neoclassical taste imported with Italian Wars veterans and artists.
polities.philosophy: Montaigne’s Pyrrhonian skepticism and essayistic self-scrutiny reshape moral philosophy outside the schools. Ramus contests Aristotelian method in the university; Stoic constancy literature coaches nobles through massacre years. Essayistic skepticism becomes a French specialty: doubt as moral method rather than university disputation alone. Neostoic constancy manuals coach nobles through massacre years.
polities.science: Ambroise Paré remakes battlefield surgery; Jacques Cartier’s and later voyages feed geographic curiosity even when politics look inward. Royal collèges and printing spread mathematical and medical texts; fortification engineers import Italian trace italienne along threatened frontiers. Trace italienne bastions and surgical practice move faster than faculties—war as research program. Royal fortifiers and royal surgeons learn faster from sieges than from commentaries.

polities.name: Kingdom of England
polities.description: England opens 1400 still claiming the French crown; Castillon (1453) ends the continental dream as the Wars of the Roses consume the nobility. Henry VII and Henry VIII rebuild monarchy on stronger fiscal and statutory footing; the break with Rome nationalizes the church and dissolves monasteries. Mary’s Catholic restoration fails to reverse the Protestant settlement that Elizabeth crafts after 1559. The Armada year (1588) and Irish wars advertise a naval-commercial kingdom projecting into the Atlantic while Calais—the last French bridgehead—falls in 1558. By 1600 Shakespeare’s London and the East India Company’s charter sit atop a still-fragile Tudor state awaiting James VI’s personal union.
polities.conflicts: Hundred Years’ War; Wars of the Roses; Anglo-Scottish border wars; Tudor reconquest and plantation pressures in Ireland; war with Spain (Armada 1588 and after); interventions in the Dutch Revolt and French Wars of Religion; privateering in the Atlantic. Privateers blur war and commerce until Spanish treasure fleets become English political weather.
polities.leaders: Henry IV; Henry V; Henry VI; Edward IV; Richard III; Henry VII; Henry VIII; Edward VI; Mary I; Elizabeth I; ministers Wolsey, Cromwell, Cecil, Walsingham.
polities.religion: Late medieval Catholicism with Lollard undercurrents yields to Henrician schism, Edwardian Protestantism, Marian restoration, and Elizabethan settlement—a via media enforced by Uniformity, with Puritan pressure and Catholic recusancy as permanent tensions. Vernacular Bible and Book of Common Prayer reshape literacy and identity.
polities.culture: Print, parish literacy, and the Book of Common Prayer reshape speech and week. Tudor court humanism, London theaters, and joint-stock venturing invent a commercial-political public. Sumptuary display and progresses teach loyalty as spectacle. Progresses, prodigy houses, and parish registers make Tudor rule visible week by week.
polities.summary: Lancastrian England opens the century still claiming the French crown; defeat in France (1453) coincides with the Wars of the Roses. Tudor consolidation under Henry VII and Henry VIII remakes church and state—Break with Rome, dissolution of…
polities.story: Agincourt (1415) is the high theatrical crest of Lancastrian France; Joan of Arc and Charles VII erase it within a generation, and Castillon closes Gascony. Towton, Tewkesbury, and Bosworth turn succession into slaughter until Henry Tudor marries the rose factions together and rebuilds solvency. Henry VIII’s matrimonial crisis becomes a constitutional revolution: supremacy statute, dissolved abbeys, and a Bible in English that outlives every Tudor face. Elizabeth’s regime survives northern Catholic revolt, Mary Stuart’s claim, and Philip II’s Armada—then spends blood and treasure on Ireland’s Nine Years’ War while London’s stages invent the nation aloud.
polities.literature: Malory compiles Arthurian loss; Tyndale’s Bible vernacularizes scripture; Spenser allegorizes empire in The Faerie Queene. Marlowe and Shakespeare make the history play a national mirror; by 1600 the stage is England’s loudest political philosophy. The history play turns chronicle into public argument about succession and counsel.
polities.art:
Perpendicular Gothic finale; Holbein’s ambassadorial realism; Elizabethan portrait miniatures (Hillier/Hilliard); prodigy houses; armada tapestries and Protestant print imagery.

Royal supremacy over the church; parliamentary statute as instrument of Reformation; Foxe’s martyrology as Protestant national memory; Hakluyt’s promotional geography for empire.
polities.ideas: Common-law constitutionalism and parliamentary statute become tools of Reformation. Richard Hooker defends an English church of reason and order; Hakluyt sells overseas expansion as Protestant duty. Parliamentary statute and common-law custom become Reformation’s toolkit—national church as legal artifact. Empire-as-duty enters sermon and pamphlet before it enters map rooms.

polities.philosophy: Humanist education (Colette, More, Erasmus’s English friends) debates conscience vs crown—More dies on the edge of that argument. Later Elizabethan Neoplatonism and Stoic counsel literature school courtiers in fortune’s wheel. Conscience vs statute remains England’s open philosophical wound after More.
polities.science: John Dee mixes mathematics, navigation, and imperial mystique; Digges and Recorde spread geometry in English. Magnetic philosophy (Gilbert) and practical seamanship underwrite Atlantic ambition more than university chairs do. Magnetic philosophy and practical seamanship matter more to empire than any single college chair. Navigational mathematics schools pilots for seas the universities barely name.

polities.name: Kingdom of Scotland
polities.description: The Auld Alliance binds Scotland to France against England; Flodden (1513) guts a generation of nobles around James IV. Minorities, regencies, and English Rough Wooing keep the realm unstable until the Reformation Parliament of 1560 overturns the old church. Mary Queen of Scots’ Catholic personal rule ends in deposition and English captivity; her son James VI learns kingcraft as a Protestant monarch. In 1603 he inherits England—personal union, not incorporating union—while Highland and Borders worlds still run on kinship and raid.
polities.conflicts: Border wars with England; Flodden; Rough Wooing; magnate feuds; Reformation crisis and Marian civil wars; entanglement in French and English succession politics. Rough Wooing burnings teach that Reformation geopolitics arrives on English horses.
polities.leaders: James I–VI Stewarts; regents Albany and Morton; Mary Queen of Scots; John Knox (prophetic opposition); Bothwell; leading earls (Huntly, Moray).
polities.religion: Medieval Catholic church → Protestant Reformation led by Knox; Presbyterian kirk structures consolidate after 1560; Catholic Highland and noble holdouts persist. Kirk sessions invent discipline as local government; bishops become a later argument.
polities.culture: Lowland Scots literary culture and burgh schools; Highland Gaelic lordship; universities at St Andrews, Glasgow, Aberdeen; martial Borders reiving tradition. Burgh schools and tower houses split Lowland literacy from Highland kinship power.
polities.summary: Stewart Scotland remains an independent kingdom bound by the Auld Alliance to France against England. James IV’s disaster at Flodden (1513), the Rough Wooing, and Reformation turmoil under Mary Queen of Scots fracture elite politics; James…
polities.story: Flodden’s billhooks (1513) end James IV’s Renaissance chivalry in a single afternoon and orphan a kingdom to regents and English pressure. John Knox’s return and the Lords of the Congregation pull Scotland into Geneva’s orbit; French troops and English intervention make reform a geopolitical bargain sealed in 1560. Mary’s marriages, Darnley’s murder, and Langside ruin turn queenship into cautionary epic; her son James VI learns kingcraft as a Protestant monarch who still writes verse. In 1603 he inherits England—personal union, not incorporating union—carrying kirk discipline and Borders memory into a wider British problem.
polities.literature: Makars (Dunbar, Henryson) adorn Stewart courts; Buchanan’s Latin and vernacular polemics school James VI; ballads remember Flodden and kin-slaying. Ballads remember Flodden more accurately than many Latin epitaphs.
polities.art:
Late Gothic burgh kirks; royal palaces (Stirling, Linlithgow, Holyrood) with French and Flemish craft; portraits of Mary and James; tower-houses as lairdly architecture.

Buchanan’s resistance theory and royal education tracts; kirk claims to independent discipline; James VI’s True Law of Free Monarchies asserting divine-right reply.
polities.ideas: Resistance theory from Knox and Buchanan haunts later British politics; covenanting language begins to fuse nation, kirk, and contract. Resistance theory from Knox/Buchanan becomes Scotland’s dangerous export.
polities.artIdeas:
Late Gothic burgh kirks; royal palaces (Stirling, Linlithgow, Holyrood) with French and Flemish craft; portraits of Mary and James; tower-houses as lairdly architecture.

Buchanan’s resistance theory and royal education tracts; kirk claims to independent discipline; James VI’s True Law of Free Monarchies asserting divine-right reply.
polities.philosophy: Scholastic universities meet humanist Latin; Buchanan’s republican-tinged pedagogy shapes a king who will later preach divine right. Humanist Latin and kirk theology share the same cramped college rooms.
polities.science: University medicine and law remain modest; practical military engineering and cartography of the Borders matter more than courts of science. Border surveying and artillery practicalities outrun speculative science.

polities.name: Crown of Castile
polities.description: Castile’s fifteenth century opens with noble civil war and weak kings (John II, Henry IV) before Isabella’s contested accession. Her partnership with Ferdinand of Aragon (1479) does not erase Castilian law or Cortes, but it pools armies for Granada’s conquest (1492). That year also launches Atlantic projection and the expulsion of Jews—twin signatures of a confessionalizing crusader crown. After 1500 the map’s Spanish Monarchy polity carries the dynastic union; Castile remains its tax base, infantry reservoir, and language of empire.
polities.conflicts: Reconquista vs Granada; Castilian civil wars; Portuguese border clashes; dynastic contests preceding Isabella; early Italian and North African forays. Frontier cabalgadas continue until Granada’s guns make raid obsolete.
polities.leaders: John II; Álvaro de Luna; Henry IV; Isabella I; Ferdinand (as consort in Castile); cardinal Mendoza; Columbus as crown agent.
polities.religion: Militant Catholicism; military orders; large Jewish and Muslim populations under rising pressure culminating in 1492 expulsion and later forced conversions. Military orders and Inquisitors share a crusading vocabulary against Jews, Muslims, and dissent.
polities.culture: Castilian vernacular prestige, court chronicles, Mudejar hybrid aesthetics, and a frontier ideology of reconquest that later justifies conquest overseas. Romance frontiers and court chronicles train Castilians to narrate conquest as vocation.
polities.summary: Trastámara Castile is the demographic and military engine of Iberia’s final Reconquista. Dynastic crisis under John II and Henry IV precedes Isabella’s contested accession; her marriage to Ferdinand of Aragon (1469) creates the Catholic Mon…
polities.story: Isabella’s marriage is a coup against partition: Castilian succession crisis resolved by a partnership that still keeps realms plural under one bed. The War of Granada is slow siegecraft—artillery, starvation, and vassal bargaining—until Boabdil yields the Alhambra on 2 January 1492. Columbus’s first voyage, funded in that victory’s afterglow, redirects Castilian crusading energy westward even as Sephardic expulsion begins. The Inquisition, already active before 1492, becomes the crown’s instrument of confessional uniformity as infantry and silver make Castile Europe’s engine.
polities.literature: Jorge Manrique’s Coplas mourn estate and death; romancero ballads recycle frontier war; Nebrija’s grammar (1492) claims language as empire’s companion. Ballad and grammar arrive together—empire wanting a language.
polities.art:
Isabelline Gothic; Mudéjar plaster and brick; Hispano-Flemish painting; fortress-palaces of the Reconquista endgame.

Neo-Gothic crusading ideology; royal-Inquisition partnership as state-building; debates on just title in the Indies beginning at century’s turn.
polities.ideas: Nebrija’s linguistic imperialism; scholastic just-war arguments around conquest; Isabeline sacral queenship as political theology. Language-as-empire (Nebrija) is Castile’s sharpest soft-power idea.
polities.artIdeas:
Isabelline Gothic; Mudéjar plaster and brick; Hispano-Flemish painting; fortress-palaces of the Reconquista endgame.

polities.philosophy: Thomist university culture (Salamanca) prepares the ground for later School of Salamanca debates on dominion and rights. Salamanca’s classrooms already rehearse doubts later aimed at the Indies.
polities.science: Cartographic and navigational knowledge concentrates in Atlantic ports; artillery and siege engineering decide Granada’s endgame. Siege trains and Atlantic pilotage are Castile’s applied sciences of 1492.

polities.name: Crown of Aragon
polities.description: Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia, the Balearics, Sardinia, Sicily, and (under Alfonso V) Naples form a contractualist thalassocracy as much as a land kingdom. Alfonso the Magnanimous’s Neapolitan court is an early Renaissance node; Catalan and Aragonese merchants stitch the western Mediterranean. Ferdinand II’s marriage to Isabella links crowns without dissolving fueros and Corts. After 1500 the Spanish Monarchy entry represents the dynastic union on the map, but Aragonese constitutional memory remains a brake on Castilian uniformity.
polities.conflicts: Italian ambitions vs Angevins and Italian states; Mediterranean rivalry with Genoa and later Ottomans; Castilian alliance/union politics; internal urban revolts. Corsair and Ottoman pressure make the inland sea a second frontier beside Castile.
polities.leaders: Ferdinand I of Aragon; Alfonso V the Magnanimous; John II; Ferdinand II the Catholic; Germaine of Foix (brief second marriage politics).
polities.religion: Catholic with significant Jewish and Muslim communities under intensifying Inquisitorial pressure after union with Castile. Convivencia memory collapses under Inquisitorial pressure after dynastic union.
polities.culture: Catalan-Aragonese commercial urbanism; Mediterranean court culture at Naples; fueros/Corts contractualism as political identity. Corts and fueros are culture—politics performed as legal theater.
polities.summary: A Mediterranean composite crown—Aragon, Catalonia, Valencia, Balearics, Sardinia, Sicily, and (from Alfonso V) Naples—oriented to trade and Italian politics as much as Iberia. Ferdinand II’s marriage to Isabella links it to Castile without…
polities.story: The Compromise of Caspe (1412) shows elective-contractual habits inside dynasty—Aragon’s political DNA. Alfonso V’s conquest of Naples exports Iberian power into the Italian Wars’ prelude and plants a Magnanimous court of humanists beside Castel Nuovo’s arch. Ferdinand’s Italy and Navarre policies braid Mediterranean strategy with Castilian armies without erasing Catalan and Valencian fueros. Germanías and local revolts remind rulers that the Crown of Aragon is a mosaic of laws, not a Castilian province with coastline.
polities.literature: Ausiàs March’s Catalan lyric; Tirant lo Blanch’s chivalric modernity; Neapolitan humanist Latin under Alfonso V. Catalan lyric and chivalric prose prove vernacular prestige without Castilian monopoly.
polities.art:
Catalan Gothic; Mediterranean Gothic–Renaissance hybrid in Naples; altarpieces and mercantile chapel art in Barcelona and Valencia.

Pactism—king bound by realm’s laws and Corts; consulate of the sea as commercial legal order; Italian humanist kingship imported via Naples.
polities.ideas: Pactism—kingship bound by realm’s laws—becomes Aragon’s durable political idea against absolutist fashion. Pactism remains Aragon’s answer to absolutist fashion.
polities.artIdeas:

polities.philosophy: Legal humanism and scholastic faculties in university towns; Neapolitan academy culture under Alfonso. Naples under Alfonso briefly becomes a philosophical court in Iberian colors.
polities.science: Portolan literacy, cartography, and commercial arithmetic of Catalan-Valencian merchants; naval architecture for Mediterranean galleys. Portolan and commercial arithmetic are Aragonese sciences of distance.

polities.name: Nasrid Emirate of Granada
polities.description: Paying parias and playing Castilian factions against each other, the Nasrids sustain a refined court under existential siege. Internal coups (Abu l-Hasan, Boabdil, al-Zagal) weaken resistance just as Isabella and Ferdinand unify Christian pressure. The war of 1482–92 is a sequence of sieges; the Alhambra’s surrender closes al-Andalus as a political project. Mudéjar and Morisco afterlives continue under Christian rule, but the emirate itself exits the map.
polities.conflicts: Defensive wars and raids vs Castile; dynastic coups inside the Nasrid house; final War of Granada (1482–1492). Parias and raids buy years; artillery spends them.
polities.leaders: Yusuf I and Muhammad V (earlier florescence still defining the palace); Muley Hacén; Boabdil (Muhammad XII); rival clan factions (Abencerrajes in legend).
polities.religion: Sunni Islam of a frontier emirate; Sufi currents; dhimmi Christian and Jewish communities under rising pressure as Castilian war intensifies; post-1492 forced conversions loom just beyond the surrender.
polities.culture: Nasrid court etiquette, Arabic poetry, agricultural sophistication in the vega, and a diplomacy of tribute and marriage with Castile. Court etiquette and agricultural wealth of the vega contradict ‘decline’ stereotypes until the end.
polities.summary: Last Muslim polity on the Iberian Peninsula, paying parias and playing Castile against itself from the Alhambra. Internal Nasrid factionalism and Castilian–Aragonese unity under the Catholic Monarchs end the emirate in 1492—closing eight ce…
polities.story: The Alhambra’s inscriptions call the palace a pearl—architecture as theology of paradise under pressure, water and stucco as statecraft. Boabdil’s factional captivity and restoration become Castile’s lever; Málaga and Baza fall to gunpowder and hunger while court poets still rhyme on the walls. 2 January 1492: keys change hands; within months Columbus sails and Sephardic expulsion begins—Granada’s end as Europe’s hinge year. Mudéjar hands keep building for Christian masters; the emirate’s political Islam exits the map, not the peninsula’s memory.
polities.literature: Court panegyric and epigraphic poetry literally written onto palace walls; later Morisco aljamiado keeps memory under conquest. Wall poetry makes literature inseparable from architecture.
polities.art:
Alhambra’s Court of the Lions and Hall of the Ambassadors; stucco muqarnas; tile mosaic; Generalife gardens—Islamic art’s Iberian late masterpiece.

Courtly adab under constriction; political fatalism and faction as themes of decline; frontier diplomacy as survival art.
polities.ideas: Royal legitimacy framed through Quranic kingship ideals and Andalusi legal schools under terminal military stress. Tributary kingship as survival strategy—politics without illusions.
polities.artIdeas:
Alhambra’s Court of the Lions and Hall of the Ambassadors; stucco muqarnas; tile mosaic; Generalife gardens—Islamic art’s Iberian late masterpiece.

polities.science: Irrigation hydraulics, astronomy inherited from Andalusi tradition, and fortress engineering against gunpowder sieges. Hydraulics of palace and orchard are Nasrid engineering at its calmest under siege.

polities.name: Spanish Monarchy (Castile–Aragon / Habsburg Spain)
polities.description: Ferdinand and Isabella’s union, Granada’s fall, and Charles V’s Burgundian-Habsburg inheritance create a monarchy spanning Iberia, Italy, the Netherlands, and the Americas. Philip II rules from the Escorial as bureaucratic-Catholic absolute theater; Lepanto (1571) crowns naval crusade, while the Armada (1588) and Dutch Revolt expose limits. The Iberian Union (1580) adds Portugal’s empire under one Habsburg without erasing Portuguese law. On this atlas Iberia, Italian holdings, and—mapped separately—the Netherlands show European weight; silver pays tercios until credit cracks.

Lepanto (1571) briefly sacralizes Mediterranean victory; the Armada’s wreck (1588) sacralizes English deliverance without ending Spanish empire. The Morisco revolt (1568–71) shows unfinished conquest inside Spain itself—empire’s frontier running through Andalusian villages.

Cabral’s Brazil landfall and the Estado da Índia make Lisbon a spice capital. Sebastian’s disaster at Alcácer Quibir (1578) orphans the dynasty; Philip II wins the 1580 succession. Through 1600 Portugal stays mapped as itself—laws, language, and Asian networks under Habsburg kings.

Vasco da Gama’s arrival at Calicut detonates Venetian spice rents; Albuquerque’s forts nail choke points from Hormuz to Malacca. Camões later epicizes the voyage; in real time it is scurvy, negotiation, and naval gunfire along monsoon routes. Sebastian’s empty throne after Alcácer Quibir (1578) invites Madrid—Iberian Union without cultural fusion, Portuguese law still speaking in its own voice.

polities.name: Kingdom of Navarre
polities.description: Navarre balances between France and Spain until Ferdinand invades Upper Navarre (1512). Lower Navarre north of the mountains passes through Foix-Albret into the hands of Jeanne d’Albret, a Calvinist queen, and her son Henry. Henry of Navarre’s French succession claim becomes the Wars of Religion’s endgame; as Henry IV he folds Navarrese royal dignity into the French crown. Fueros and Basque-Romance frontier customs outlive full sovereignty.
polities.conflicts: Caught between France and Spain; 1512 Castilian invasion; later French dynastic-religious wars. Partition itself is the long war—Spain south, French dynastic gravity north.
polities.leaders: Charles III; Blanche I; John II of Aragon (consort/king); Catherine of Foix; Henry II d’Albret; Jeanne d’Albret; Henry III of Navarre (IV of France).
polities.religion: Catholic Upper Navarre under Spain; Jeanne’s Calvinism in the north; Henry’s pragmatic conversion for France. Calvinist Béarn vs Catholic Upper Navarre makes the Pyrenees a confessional border.
polities.culture: Basque and Romance vernaculars; customary law (fueros); mountain pastoral and cross-Pyrenean trade. Customary law is Navarre’s culture hero.
polities.summary: Pyrenean kingdom partitioned by Spanish conquest of Upper Navarre (1512). The rump north of the mountains passes through Foix-Albret to Henry of Navarre, who becomes Henry IV of France—carrying a small realm’s title into Bourbon greatness.
polities.story: 1512’s Spanish invasion is strategic cleanup during Italian Wars logistics—Upper Navarre folded south while the Pyrenees keep a rump alive. Jeanne d’Albret makes Béarn a Reformed laboratory, printing godly magistracy into mountain politics. Her son Henry’s ‘Paris is worth a Mass’ is Navarrese survival instinct scaled to millions: a Pyrenean kingship that ends as the Bourbon dawn of France. Fueros and Basque-Romance custom outlive full sovereignty as the kingdom’s lasting constitution.
polities.literature: Court and Calvinist polemical print in Béarn; later Bourbon mythmaking absorbs Navarre into French royal story. Polemic print in a small kingdom punches above its size.

polities.name: Burgundian State
polities.description: Philip the Bold’s line builds a princely empire of Flanders cloth cities, Brabant, Holland, and the dual Burgundian duchies—ceremony rivaling kings. Philip the Good’s Golden Fleece and court feasts set European aristocratic fashion; Charles the Bold overreaches against Swiss and Lorraine. Nancy (1477) kills him; Louis XI seizes the duchy proper while Mary of Burgundy’s Habsburg marriage transfers the Low Countries to Austria/Spain. Burgundy as independent great power exits; its cultural software—chivalry, oil painting, court ritual—infects Europe.
polities.conflicts: Armagnac–Burgundian civil war; wars with Louis XI; Swiss wars (Grandson, Murten, Nancy 1476–77); Liège repressions. Urban revolts (Liège) and Swiss pikes bookend Valois Burgundy’s violence.
polities.leaders: Philip the Bold; John the Fearless; Philip the Good; Charles the Bold; Mary of Burgundy; Maximilian of Habsburg as consort.
polities.religion: Catholic magnificence—chantries, charterhouses (Champmol), and civic devotion in Flemish towns. Charterhouse piety and civic processions fund a Catholic magnificence without a kingdom’s title.
polities.culture: Court of Dijon/Bruges as school of Europe; urban guild power; chivalric orders; Netherlandish luxury trades. The ‘theater state’ of feast and order becomes Europe’s aristocratic curriculum.

Mary’s Habsburg marriage transfers the Netherlands; the duchy proper falls to Louis XI—state dead, style immortal.

polities.description: From late Luxemburg/Habsburg emperors through Charles V, the Reich remains a legal-political order of estates, not a centralized kingdom. Imperial cities, electors, and territorial princes bargain via diets; the Golden Bull’s skeleton still structures elections. Luther’s revolt (1517+) and the Peasants’ War, then princely Protestant leagues, split the Empire confessionally; Augsburg 1555 freezes cuius regio. Akhmat Khan’s stand on the Ugra (1480) fails to restore suzerainty over Moscow; by 1502 Crimea destroys the Great Horde’s remnant. The map’s Horde is a fading claim more than a stable empire.
polities.conflicts: Internal succession wars; aftermath of Timur’s devastation; wars with Muscovy and Lithuania; rivalry with Crimean Khanate. Frontier fortresses and mercenary contracts turn diplomacy into a permanent armed negotiation.
polities.leaders: Tokhtamysh (earlier memory); Ahmed Khan; various short-lived khans of the Great Horde; Crimean rivals who inherit the western claim.
polities.religion: Sunni Islam since the fourteenth century; steppe Islamic-urban hybrids at Sarai’s memory. Confession becomes administrative identity as much as belief—parish registers and diets enforcing the map of faith.
polities.culture: Turko-Mongol aristocratic tradition; tribute politics; caravan-steppe commercial residues. Court ceremony, urban guilds, and print shops remake who can speak for the polity.
polities.summary: Fragmenting Jochid successor still claiming suzerainty over Rus’ princes into the 15th century. Great Stand on the Ugra (1480) symbolizes Muscovy’s emancipation; the Great Horde collapses under Crimean and Muscovite blows by the early 1500s…
polities.story: Tokhtamysh’s earlier wars with Timur leave a weakened steppe empire of quarreling heirs and fading Sarai. Fifteenth-century succession strife produces Crimean, Kazan, Astrakhan, and Great Horde fragments claiming one Chinggisid prestige. Akhmat Khan’s stand on the Ugra (1480) fails to restore suzerainty over Moscow—two armies stare, then the Horde withdraws. By 1502 Crimea destroys the Great Horde’s remnant; a world of tribute yields to gunpowder empires and fortified Orthodoxy.
polities.literature: Turkic-Mongol oral and chancery residues; Islamic historiography of Jochid lines. Vernacular and Latin compete to own memory: chronicle, pamphlet, and song.
polities.art:
Portable steppe arts—metalwork, textiles, horse gear; architectural echoes at Sarai’s fading sites; Islamic urban craft in surviving towns.

Chinggisid supremacy claims; tribute as world order; fragmentation into regional khanates as new political logic.
polities.ideas: Chinggisid charisma as legitimacy after territorial loss—a politics of blood and memory. Political thought here is local first—law, estate, and dynasty before abstract ‘Europe’.

polities.philosophy: Islamic legal norms adapted to nomadic-imperial rule; practical steppe statecraft. Schools and courts import humanism unevenly; practical ethics often outrun metaphysics.
polities.science: Cavalry logistics; census-tribute techniques; urban decline limiting scholarly institutions by the late phase. Applied arts of war, navigation, mining, or calendar reform count as the century’s hard knowledge.
